title: A cross-engine geometry test draws the same named shape from three kernels and asks whether they agree
summary: Each named test shape (box, cone, torus, revolved nozzle, ...) is built once by a Gmsh/OpenCASCADE-style boundary-representation kernel, a PicoGK-compatible voxel kernel and a signed-distance-field kernel, tessellated, and drawn in the same viewer. The figure is a visual agreement check: if the three renderings coincide, the shapes are the same to drawing accuracy. Numbers (volume, bounding box, distance between surfaces) are the next, stronger test.

source.note: Representative figure: the SDF-kernel revolved nozzle. The group is 45 figures: 15 Gmsh, 14 PicoGK-compatible and 16 SDF-kernel renderings of the same shape list (the SDF kernel adds a sphere and an implicit-only smooth blend; PicoGK has no step round trip). The page does not state tolerances, mesh sizes or any numerical comparison; those are not claimed here.

read_the_figure.question: Do independent geometry engines produce the same solid when given the same description?
read_the_figure.axes: A 3D matplotlib view of the triangulated surface. For the nozzle, x runs from 0 to about 0.07, and y and z each from about -0.02 to 0.02 (units are not printed; metres is the natural reading for a flow nozzle). The title names the kernel and the shape: 'sdf: revolved_nozzle'. The axes are plain coordinates, so the same view angle and limits across the group make the pictures directly comparable.
look_at: The silhouette: a wide cylinder on the left, a straight conical contraction, then a narrower cylinder on the right ending in a flat disc. A revolved profile has circular cross-sections everywhere.
The facets. Thin lines run along the length: the circle is approximated by straight segments, so you see the tessellation of each kernel, not the exact surface.
The kinks. Between wide cylinder and cone, and between cone and narrow cylinder, the surface changes slope abruptly. Those two rings must be at the same x in every kernel.
Compare against the Gmsh and PicoGK-compatible nozzles in the group: same title format, same axes. At the drawn resolution the three nozzles look identical; the facet pattern can differ in detail.
For shapes with holes or curvature (box minus cylinder, torus, tube), check that the hole is a through hole and that the curved parts are smooth to the eye.
read_the_figure.proves: That, to the accuracy of a rendered picture, the three engines interpret the same shape recipe identically: same extent on each axis, same feature positions, same topology (through holes stay through holes). It does not prove equal volume, surface area or watertightness. Those need a numerical comparison.
if_wrong: A different extent on one axis: a unit, scaling or placement convention differs between kernels (for example a primitive centred versus placed at the origin).
A missing or filled feature (a hole that is not cut): a Boolean operation failed or was applied in the wrong order.
Visibly faceted curved surface in one kernel only: a coarser tessellation or voxel size, which will show up as a volume deficit rather than a geometric disagreement.
A jagged, stair-stepped surface: a voxel kernel at too coarse a voxel size.
Holes or missing triangles in the shaded surface: a non-watertight mesh, which breaks any later volume or meshing step.
must_check: The same view angle and axis limits in every panel, otherwise the pictures are not comparable. Here they match.
A quantitative companion: bounding box, enclosed volume, surface area and a surface-to-surface distance. Not printed on these figures.
The tessellation tolerance (chord error or voxel size) is stated, so that a small difference can be judged as discretization or as a real bug.
The comparison includes shapes that stress different operations: Booleans, revolve, sweep, transform, and a file round trip.

terms.meaning: A solid stored as its bounding faces, edges and vertices, each with exact geometry (planes, cylinders, splines). CAD kernels such as OpenCASCADE work this way; Gmsh uses one for its geometry module.
A function d(x) giving the distance to the surface, negative inside and positive outside. The surface is the set d = 0.
A solid stored as a grid of small cells with values (inside/outside or distance). PicoGK is a voxel-based kernel; 'PicoGK-compatible' here means a kernel following its voxel approach.
Replacing a curved surface by flat triangles so that it can be drawn or meshed. Every picture in this group shows a tessellation.
Turning a field into a triangle mesh by finding where it crosses a level, usually zero (marching cubes is the standard algorithm). It is how an SDF or voxel solid becomes a drawable surface.
A solid made by sweeping a 2D profile around an axis. The nozzle is a profile of three segments revolved about the x axis.
Union, intersection and difference of solids. With SDFs they are min and max of the fields.
Export a shape to a file (STEP or STL), read it back, and compare with the original. It tests that nothing is lost in the file format.
The largest distance from any point on one surface to the nearest point of the other: a standard single number for 'how different are these two shapes'.

remember: Three representations, one shape: exact faces (B-rep), a distance function (SDF), a grid of cells (voxels).
Agreement of pictures is necessary, not sufficient. Pictures are tessellated; equal pictures can hide a few percent of volume.
A faceted circle with N sides has area (N / 2 pi) sin(2 pi / N) of the true disc. It is always smaller; the deficit falls as 1 / N squared.
Any difference between kernels is either a convention difference (units, origin), a failed operation, or a discretization effect. Classify it before fixing it.
For SDF solids, union is min, intersection is max, difference is max(a, -b). Away from the surface these are not true distances, only valid fields.
understand: The group is a test matrix: rows are shapes (box, cone, torus, nozzle, ...), columns are kernels. A cross-check is strong because the engines share no code: a bug would have to appear identically in three independent implementations to go unseen.

Shapes are chosen to stress different operations. Box and cylinder test primitives; box minus cylinder tests a Boolean; the nozzle and torus test revolve and curvature; the L profile and L channel test extrusion and a concave corner; the translated and rotated assembly tests rigid transforms; the STEP and STL round trips test file I/O; the vessel tube figure is a further tube-type test shape.

The smooth blend of two spheres exists only in the SDF kernel, because it uses a smooth minimum, which has no equivalent in B-rep Booleans. It is the one figure in the group with no cross-check partner.

steps.title: The nozzle as a revolved profile
steps.note: A solid of revolution about the x axis has circular sections of radius r(x). The nozzle profile r(x) is piecewise: constant, linear, constant. Any kernel must reproduce r(x) at every x.

steps.title: Volume of the three pieces
steps.note: Cylinder, conical frustum, cylinder. The frustum term follows from integrating r(x)^2 for a linear r(x). This is the number a quantitative cross-check would compare across kernels.

steps.title: An SDF solid: sphere, and Boolean algebra
steps.tex: d_{\mathrm{sphere}}(\mathbf{x})=\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}\rVert-\rho,\qquad d_{A\cup B}=\operatorname{min}(d_A,d_B),\quad d_{A\cap B}=\operatorname{max}(d_A,d_B),\quad d_{A\setminus B}=\operatorname{max}(d_A,-d_B)
steps.note: Negative inside, zero on the surface. Boolean operations are pointwise min and max, so the SDF kernel builds the box-minus-cylinder shape without any face-intersection geometry.

steps.title: Smooth union: the blended spheres
steps.note: A smooth minimum (one common form). As k goes to 0 it becomes the sharp min; for larger k it rounds the crease where two spheres meet, as in the smooth-blend figure. A B-rep kernel would need an explicit fillet operation.

steps.title: From field to the triangles you see
steps.note: Field-based (SDF and voxel) solids are typically drawn by extracting the zero level set. The mesh vertices lie within about one cell width of the true surface, which is why the cell size is the accuracy of the comparison.

steps.title: Tessellation is a controlled error
steps.note: For a circle approximated by N inscribed chords. N = 64 loses about 0.16 percent of the area and N = 32 about 0.64 percent (checked by computation). Two kernels with different N disagree by about this much even when both are right.

steps.title: A number for 'the same shape'
steps.tex: d_{H}(A,B)=\operatorname{max}\!\left\{\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,\;\sup_{b\in B}\inf_{a\in A}\lVert a-b\rVert\right\}
steps.note: Compare d_H with the tessellation tolerance. If d_H is of the order of one cell or one chord error, the kernels agree; if it is of the order of a feature size, they do not.

worked.title: Volume of a nozzle of this shape
worked.problem: Illustrative round numbers, not the project's values: wide radius R = 0.02, narrow radius r = 0.01, wide length L1 = 0.03, taper length h = 0.01, narrow length L3 = 0.02 (all in the same length unit). What is the enclosed volume, and how much smaller is a 64-sided tessellation?

solution.text: Sum, then the tessellation factor for N = 64 applies to each circular section's area.

worked.answer: V is about 5.13e-5 cubic units and the 64-gon mesh holds about 0.16 percent less. A cross-check tolerance tighter than that is meaningless unless the tessellations are identical.

analyze.q: Three kernels give nozzles whose pictures coincide, but the enclosed volumes differ by 2 percent. List the possible causes and the check that separates them.
analyze.hint: Tessellation versus voxel size versus a real geometric difference; compute d_H.

analyze.q: The SDF and voxel kernels extract a surface by iso-surfacing, the B-rep kernel by tessellating exact faces. Which would you expect to be more faceted along the nozzle's curved cross-sections, and where would sharp edges be rounded?
analyze.hint: Sharp rings are the places a regular grid cannot resolve exactly.

analyze.q: Why does the cross-check include a STEP and an STL round trip as separate shapes?
analyze.hint: STEP stores exact geometry, STL stores triangles.

evaluate.q: Is a visual match across 45 figures adequate evidence that the three kernels agree? State the minimum extra evidence.
evaluate.hint: Volume, bounding box, d_H, and the tolerance of each kernel.

evaluate.q: Shapes were chosen by hand. What classes of geometry would this test set not catch?
evaluate.hint: Thin walls, near-tangent surfaces, very large aspect ratio, self-intersection.

create: Design a numeric companion table for this group: one row per shape, columns for bounding box, volume, surface area and d_H against the B-rep kernel, with a pass tolerance tied to the tessellation size.
Add two shapes that would stress the kernels more than the current ones (for example a thin shell and two near-tangent spheres) and state what failure you expect from each kernel type.

checks.q: Why use three independent kernels rather than one?
checks.answer: Because independent implementations rarely share a bug. If all three produce the same shape, the shape recipe is probably interpreted correctly; if one differs, the difference localises the problem to that kernel or to a convention.

checks.q: A circle is drawn with 128 chords. Roughly what fraction of its area is lost?
checks.answer: About 0.04 percent (the ratio is 0.99960 as computed).

checks.q: Gmsh and SDF nozzles look the same, but the SDF one has slightly rounded rings where the cone starts. What does that suggest?
checks.hint: Where does a regular grid struggle?
checks.answer: Discretization at the sharp edges, from the cell size or the smoothing of iso-surface extraction. It is a resolution effect, not a different design, and it should shrink as the cell size is reduced.

checks.q: Two kernels differ in surface distance by one cell width. Pass or fail?
checks.hint: What is the best accuracy a grid kernel can claim?
checks.answer: Pass at the grid's own accuracy: one cell is the expected resolution. Fail only if the tolerance was declared tighter than the cell size, in which case the tolerance was unrealistic for that kernel.

checks.q: How would you cross-check a shape that exists only in the SDF kernel, such as the smooth blend?
checks.hint: No other kernel can build it.
checks.answer: Compare against an analytic property: the blend of two spheres must contain both spheres, be symmetric about the plane between them, and have a volume bounded between the sharp union and the sharp union plus a fillet allowance. Or build the same field in a second, independent implementation.
